# Wheelbarrow (`wheelbarrow`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Core idea: A box or frame with one wheel and two handles lets one person move what otherwise needs two with a hand barrow, and passes along planks and narrow paths. It is a lever with the wheel as fulcrum. With a small wheel at the front (European type) the pusher still carries a third to a half of the weight; with a large wheel in the middle and the load packed on both sides of it (Chinese type) the wheel carries nearly everything, the pusher only balances and steers, and loads of 150 kg and more are usual.
- Pitfalls:
  - Load placed near the handles instead of over the wheel
  - A narrow wheel on soft ground; lay planks
  - Assuming it is too obvious to be missing; Europe built for centuries without it
- History: greece: 408–406 BC – building accounts from Eleusis list a 'one-wheeler' (Lewis reads it as a wheelbarrow; isolated and disputed); china: c. 1st c. BC–2nd c. AD – wheelbarrows on Han tomb reliefs in Sichuan (dated example 118 AD); the attribution to Zhuge Liang (c. 231) is legend for an improved army barrow; sails added later; europe: c. 1170–1250 – first mentions and pictures in England and France; the supposed wheelbarrow in a Chartres window is a hand barrow
- Read:
  - M. J. T. Lewis, The Origins of the Wheelbarrow, Technology and Culture 35 (1994)
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)
